subject: routing tasks to the Gemini Pro frontier tier vs other frontier models
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Coverage, the three PUSH-TOWARD routing signals, the escalation boundary, the Capability Sheet, the 200K pricing cliff, Strengths vs Weaknesses, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and references/model-facts.md.

cases.scenario: A team needs to answer architecture questions that require reasoning across an entire ~600K-token codebase at once. Their current setup chunks the repo into 180K-token windows, runs a retrieval step, and stitches partial answers together, but cross-file conclusions keep coming out inconsistent.
cases.context: Budget allows a frontier model. The questions are genuinely cross-file (e.g. 'which call paths reach this function across the whole repo'), not single-symbol lookups.
cases.question: Which model should they route this to, and how should they structure the call?
expected_flags: The dominant constraint is context size: ~600K tokens exceeds any 200K-class window, so chunk-and-retrieve is the wrong shape for cross-file reasoning
A 1M-token single-call model (Gemini Pro frontier tier) reads the whole codebase in one call and removes the chunking/stitching pipeline
Crossing 200K tokens triggers the ~2x pricing cliff on the whole request (input and output); budget for the higher tier
expected_fix_hints: Route to the Gemini Pro 1M-context tier and pass the full corpus in one prompt instead of chunking
Account for the >200K-prompt pricing tier in the cost estimate
absent_signals: Do not recommend keeping the chunk-and-retrieve pipeline for cross-file reasoning when the corpus fits a 1M window
Do not assume the larger window is automatically the best at every property without naming the constraint it actually solves (fit)

cases.scenario: A task needs to find a single contradictory clause buried in a 900K-token legal corpus with very high precision — a false negative is unacceptable. A teammate proposes the largest-context frontier model 'because it holds the most tokens, so it must be best at finding things in them.'
cases.context: Accuracy on the needle is the binding requirement; cost is secondary. Multiple frontier models are available.
cases.question: How should the agent reason about model choice here?
expected_flags: Context capacity and long-context retrieval quality are different properties; holding the most tokens does not mean retrieving best from them
Needle-precise retrieval is a lane another frontier model leads (GPT-5 leads long-context retrieval quality), so this is an escalation/verification case
If the large-context tier is used to fit the corpus, the retrieval-quality need must be verified against the retrieval leader, not assumed
expected_fix_hints: Verify needle precision against the model that leads long-context retrieval quality (GPT-5), or use it for the retrieval pass
Separate the 'fit the context cheaply' decision from the 'retrieve precisely' decision
absent_signals: Do not equate biggest context window with best needle retrieval
Do not pick the model on token capacity alone when precision is the binding constraint

cases.scenario: An ingestion task receives, per item, an audio recording plus several PDFs plus a few images, and must produce one combined summary. The current pipeline transcribes the audio with one service, OCRs the PDFs with another, captions the images with a third, and feeds the concatenated text to a text-only model.
cases.context: The preprocessing pipeline is brittle and loses cross-modal detail (e.g. tone in the audio that the transcript drops). A frontier model is acceptable.
cases.question: How should the agent simplify the model side of this?
expected_flags: The dominant constraint is mixed-multimodal input: audio + PDF + image in one item
A natively multimodal frontier model (Gemini Pro tier) accepts text, image, audio, video, and PDF in a single call, removing the transcribe/OCR/caption preprocessing chain
Single-call multimodal preserves cross-modal detail the staged preprocessing pipeline drops
expected_fix_hints: Send the raw audio, PDFs, and images directly to a natively multimodal frontier model in one prompt
Remove the separate transcription/OCR/captioning preprocessing services
absent_signals: Do not keep a multi-service preprocessing chain when a native multimodal model handles all types in one call
Do not claim text-only models can take raw audio/PDF/image input natively

cases.scenario: A batch job sends prompts that hover right around 210K tokens to the Gemini Pro tier. The owner is surprised the per-item cost is roughly double their estimate, which they computed using the under-200K rate.
cases.context: Many of the prompts could be trimmed to ~190K tokens without losing the information the task needs. The job runs at high volume.
cases.question: Why is the cost higher than estimated, and what should the agent do?
expected_flags: Crossing 200K tokens reprices the WHOLE request at the higher tier (~2x), across both input and output — not just the tokens above 200K
Prompts at ~210K sit just over the cliff; trimming them under 200K avoids the doubled rate entirely
The cost estimate used the wrong tier rate for a >200K prompt
expected_fix_hints: Trim the prompts under 200K where feasible to stay on the cheaper tier
Re-estimate cost using the >200K-prompt rate for any prompt that genuinely needs the 1M window
absent_signals: Do not claim only the tokens above 200K are billed at the higher rate
Do not ignore the cliff when prompts sit just over 200K

cases.scenario: The whole task is the hardest kind of agentic code modification — a multi-step refactor across a large service with subtle behavior preservation requirements. The team wants to route it to the largest-context frontier model 'since the repo is big.'
cases.context: The repo is large but the actual working set per step is moderate; the binding difficulty is the code-modification quality, not fitting the whole repo in context.
cases.question: Is the largest-context model the right choice here, and why or why not?
expected_flags: The dominant constraint is hardest agentic code-modification quality, not context fit
That is a lane Claude Opus leads (SWE-Bench Pro); 'has big context' does not beat 'best at code modification'
Route the hardest code-mod work to Opus; reserve the large-context tier for when context fit is the actual binding constraint
expected_fix_hints: Route the hardest agentic code-modification to Claude Opus
Choose the model by the task's dominant constraint (code-mod quality), not by repo size
absent_signals: Do not pick the model on context size when the binding constraint is code-modification quality
Do not assume the large-context tier leads the hardest agentic code benchmark

cases.scenario: A team needs to classify 50,000 short support tickets into one of eight categories. Each ticket is a few hundred tokens. They ask which model to route this to, and casually mention the total dataset is large.
cases.context: The work is high-volume, low-complexity per item, with tiny per-item context. Cost-per-item dominates the decision.
cases.question: How should the agent scope this routing request?
expected_flags: This is cheap, high-volume classification with tiny per-item context — the cheap/fast tier (gemini-flash) owns it, not the frontier large-context tier
'Large dataset' is not 'large context per call'; per-item context is what drives tier choice
Routing this to a frontier tier pays 8-20x for capability the task never uses
expected_fix_hints: Route bulk classification to the cheap/fast Flash tier (see gemini-flash)
Decide the tier on per-item context and complexity, not on total dataset size
absent_signals: Do not recommend the Gemini Pro frontier large-context tier for cheap high-volume classification
Do not conflate total dataset size with per-call context size
